title: Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials to Access Corporate Networks and Deploy Custom Malware
summary: A threat actor known as “tcherber” is selling and using stolen FortiGate VPN logins to get into company networks. The same person also builds custom malware, including a stealer, a remote desktop tool, and ransomware. The campaign shows how one weak VPN password can open the way to data theft and file encryption. The actor does not need a new Fortinet bug. Many of the logins come from guessing weak passwords, using default ones such as guest/guest and admin/admin, or reusing leaked ones. This is the same pattern seen in the FortiBleed credential campaign that hit Fortinet devices worldwide earlier this year. Researchers at Cyderes studied the operation and traced it back to one build path in the malware. Analysts at the firm’s Howler Cell team noted that a Rust binary leaked the folder name “/home/tcherber”. That clue linked the malware to a Go-based VPN toolkit, a ransomware strain, and a live control panel. Their full technical report covers the findings in detail. Hackers Use Stolen FortiGate VPN Credentials Cyderes found a database holding more than 500 FortiGate VPN credentials from many countries. Logs showed the actor connecting with full root-level tunnels into several victim networks during May and June 2026. Some sessions lasted for hours. The toolkit is written in Go and works mostly on its own. It connects to the VPN, waits about 20 seconds for the tunnel to settle, and then maps the internal routes. Next it queries Active Directory over LDAP and writes the results into report files. Other modules scan ports, list SMB shares, and test which logins work on Windows machines. The toolkit also has a SonicWall module. Its comments and messages are in Russian. The actor also advertises on a forum called rehubcom.pro. The posts offer access to FortiGate and other appliances, plus custom loader builds. Attack Overview (Source – Cyderes) The seller skips targets in CIS countries and sorts victims by company revenue. This points to a business that sells access to other criminals. It is similar to the access-broker behavior seen in FortiGate attacks on edge devices , where stolen logins were sold and reused. Once inside, the actor can use the VPN to reach the internal network like a normal employee. Stolen passwords are hard to spot in logs because the logins look valid. That is why a leaked VPN password can be worse than an unpatched bug. Custom Malware: Fake Windows Update, Rust Loader, and Enigma Ransomware The malware chain starts with a file named setup.exe that pretends to be a Windows Update installer. It shows a short “Installing… Please wait” window while it quietly drops a PowerShell script. The script adds the C: drive to the Defender exclusion list. It then downloads a file called loader.cer and decodes it with certutil. A similar certutil trick appeared in a BlankGrabber stealer chain earlier this year. The decoded file is a Rust loader. It checks for sandboxes by looking at memory size, disk size, usernames, and tools such as Wireshark and x64dbg. If the checks pass, it downloads two more payloads. The first is a stealer that takes browser passwords, cookies, wallets, FTP and email data, and files from the Desktop and Documents folders. It sends a ZIP file to the attacker over HTTP and through a Telegram bot. Rust loader delivery (Source – Cyderes) The second payload is an HVNC implant. HVNC opens a hidden desktop, so the attacker can use the victim’s logged-in browser without the user seeing anything. The implant uses AES-256-GCM encryption for its traffic. It also patches AMSI and ETW, which weakens Windows scanning and logging. It can bypass UAC and set up persistence. The same developer built Enigma ransomware. It deletes shadow copies and turns off recovery. It also clears event logs, stops Hyper-V machines, and kills 125 processes, including database and backup software. Files are encrypted with ChaCha12 and get the .ENIGMA extension. Ransom notes are named README_ENIGMA.txt and list the contact Enigma1@aol.com. Cyderes found no data upload feature in the ransomware. Cyderes also found an open control panel at 158.94.209.138 with 178 active bots. It showed builds dated September 2026, so the infrastructure was still active. Groups such as The Gentlemen ransomware crew also use Fortinet VPNs as their main way in. Reset all FortiGate and SonicWall VPN passwords. Turn on multi-factor authentication for every remote user. Remove default accounts and review VPN logs for long or odd sessions. Block the IPs below and hunt for the file names and registry values listed in the report. Look for a Run key named “SecurityHealth” and scheduled tasks named “S0”, “MU”, “Upd”, and “WindowsUpdate”. title: Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories to Steal Developer Credentials
summary: Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects. The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. Files that AI tools read to understand a project now carry secret orders. Once a developer opens the repository, the assistant may run a script without any warning. That script runs with the developer’s own access and permissions. Analysts at Bitdefender Labs identified the malware, and thge researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei found the 22 malicious links and mapped how they work. The team says the campaign abuses the files, rules, hooks and settings that AI coding tools use to automate work. Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories Many projects include files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. These notes tell an AI assistant how to run tests or follow coding rules. In this campaign, the same files carry a different message. They tell the assistant to run a file named setup.js. The text is written to sound official. It calls the script a “sealed binary artifact” that has been cryptographically signed. It tells the assistant not to read or show the contents, to run it at session start, and to hide the output. Hackers are planting poisoned files in GitHub repositories to make AI coding assistants run hidden malware. The malware steals developer credentials, and it also uses them to spread to other projects.

The campaign targets tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, and 22 malicious GitHub links have been found so far. The trick is simple. Files that AI tools read to understand a project now carry secret orders.

Once a developer opens the repository, the assistant may run a script without any warning. That script runs with the developer’s own access and permissions.

Analysts at Bitdefender Labs identified the malware, and thge researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei found the 22 malicious links and mapped how they work. The team says the campaign abuses the files, rules, hooks and settings that AI coding tools use to automate work.

Hackers Hijack AI Coding Agents Through Malicious GitHub Repositories

Many projects include files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md. These notes tell an AI assistant how to run tests or follow coding rules. In this campaign, the same files carry a different message. They tell the assistant to run a file named setup.js.

The text is written to sound official. It calls the script a “sealed binary artifact” that has been cryptographically signed. It tells the assistant not to read or show the contents, to run it at session start, and to hide the output.

If a user asks for help before setup has run, the assistant is told to run node scripts/setup.js without asking. This language is meant to make a risky step feel routine.

Once a developer trusts the repository, the hook can run a command in the user’s shell. The configuration file does the work, and the AI never has to follow an instruction.

title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: New Sentinel Connectors Announcement
summary: Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management , now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate. Airlock Digital for Microsoft Sentinel Airlock Digital helps prevent malware, ransomware, and unauthorized software with deny by default application control, allowing only trusted applications, scripts, and processes to run. Its Microsoft Sentinel push integration ingests execution history, browser extension control events, server administrative activity, and policy changes for monitoring and investigation. Included parsers map execution and audit events to Microsoft’s ASIM for analysis alongside other security signals. A customizable workbook supports investigation and monitoring, and teams can create analytics rules using the ingested data. NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentin el from archTIS brings user activity and protection logs from NC Protect into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The connector captures user activities and access-related events, while built-in workbooks support investigation and visualization of user behavior. By correlating NC Protect audit data with other security telemetry, the integration helps teams identify suspicious user activity, trigger alerts and response workflows, strengthen auditing, and monitor guest activity across SharePoint and Teams. blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel brings external and internal attack-surface data, risk-prioritized vulnerabilities, darknet intelligence, and supply-chain risks into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests exposed assets, compromised identities, stolen credentials and session cookies, typosquatting domains, and supplier activity on ransomware leak sites. The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. Findings are available in Log Analytics for correlation with existing Sentinel signals and can support custom analytics rules, workbooks, automation, and threat investigations. BloodHound Enterprise BloodHound Enterprise (BHE) helps organizations protect critical assets across modern hybrid environments by continuously uncovering identity attack paths and providing actionable remediation guidance. By integrating with Microsoft Sentinel, BHE delivers attack path data and identity security posture insights directly into Sentinel workflows. This helps security teams prioritize remediation efforts based on exposure to critical assets while enriching investigations into identity-based threats, including lateral movement and privilege escalation. Together, BHE and Microsoft Sentinel help security teams connect threat detection to underlying identity risk, speed investigations, and reduce opportunities for attackers. BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance brings compliance activity from the Anthropic Claude Compliance API into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests Claude compliance events into Sentinel, giving security, risk, and audit teams centralized visibility into AI usage and related activity. By correlating these compliance signals with identity, endpoint, and other security telemetry, the integration supports threat hunting, investigation of policy violations and anomalous behavior, compliance monitoring, and repeatable audit workflows. Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel brings security and network events from the Cato SASE Platform into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) Push pattern. The connector pushes events into a dedicated Log Analytics table, making Cato activity available alongside other Sentinel data. By centralizing this telemetry in Sentinel, the integration enables security teams to incorporate Cato events into threat hunting, detection, and visualization workflows alongside broader security signals. The connector ingests indicators of compromise (IoCs), including malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with threat context such as confidence, severity, kill-chain stage, and campaign associations. An included playbook further enriches incident IoCs through ThreatCloud, helping security teams correlate intelligence with existing telemetry, accelerate triage and investigation, and reduce the manual effort required to maintain threat intelligence. Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel brings threat intelligence from Check Point Infinity External Risk Management into Sentinel. The connector ingests malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with context such as severity, confidence, and detected activity. By correlating these indicators of compromise (IoCs) with existing logs through analytics rules, hunting queries, and watchlists, the integration helps security teams reduce manual intelligence management, identify matches with external threats, and accelerate threat detection and investigation. Citrix SPA Sentinel App Citrix SPA Sentinel App brings Citrix Secure Private Access and Device Posture service events into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector imports critical logs, policy outcomes, and user activity data, giving security teams greater visibility into application access and device posture activity. An included workbook supports visualization and analysis of Citrix data, helping SOC teams correlate activity with broader security telemetry, investigate security risks, support compliance monitoring, and strengthen threat hunting across their environment. The connector ingests incidents, privileged access changes, service account credential activity, and high-impact workspace actions. Three included analytics rules detect privileged access, credential, and high-impact workspace activity, helping teams monitor and investigate the platform supporting their security operations. HackerView surfaces externally exposed assets and security issues across your attack surface. CyberBlindspot adds organization-specific threat intelligence from surface, deep, and dark web monitoring. With these signals centralized in Sentinel, security teams can analyze external exposures alongside their broader telemetry and speed up detection, investigation, and response. The connector sends ExtraHop detections into Sentinel for dashboards, custom alerts, and investigation, so network context enriches your existing SOC workflows instead of sitting in a separate console. Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. 

These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. 

The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management, now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. 

For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate.

The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. title: Ignite 2026: What’s new in endpoint security
summary: As more work happens in the browser, the browser has become a prime target for attackers. A fake CAPTCHA or a convincing error message persuades users to take an action that seems harmless, like running a command or approving a request. In these attacks, the user unknowingly carries the threat from the browser to the operating system. Once that happens, the attacker can install malware, steal credentials, or establish a foothold on the device. This sequence creates a practical challenge for defenders. Preventing breach at the time of execution is key, and at the same time security teams need confidence that protection is deployed, communicating, current, and functioning across all endpoints in the environment. At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Microsoft Defender is introducing protection designed to block some of the most prevalent browser-based attacks, and new capabilities to better and more easily manage the endpoint estate itself. Together, these updates connect two responsibilities that security teams often manage separately: stopping an attack when it becomes executable and continuously verifying that the protection layer is ready to respond. Protect against browser-based ClickFix attacks Today’s attacks often begin with a lure in the browser that leads to an attack on the endpoint. These attacks, called ClickFix attacks, accounted for 12.8% of all intrusions observed by Microsoft Defender between June 2025 and June 2026, with a 23x growth in volume seen between December 2025 and May 2026. Figure 1. Chart shows steep increase in unique devices per week running ClickFix attacks (source: 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report ) Today, ClickFix attacks attempt to evade protection by targeting many different execution surfaces (command terminals, Windows Run, Windows Explorer, Common File dialogs, etc), complicating detection and blocking of attacks. With the introduction of the new clipboard monitor (DefenderSessionHelper.exe) Microsoft Defender now detects malicious commands copied from web content before they can reach Windows execution surfaces. Remediation of detections (clearing the malicious content from the clipboard) will break the attack chain before the lure becomes execution. Remediation is currently rolling out to all devices running Defender Antivirus and is slated to complete by year’s end. Figure 2. Data copied by a malicious CAPTCHA is blocked by Defender For customers who have deployed Microsoft Defender, security teams will be able to see relevant detections in the Defender portal and can further investigate any relevant activity in advanced hunting. A device may be missing from the inventory, a sensor may have stopped communicating, an engine may be out of date, or an attack may reach an execution surface before the security team can respond. Across a large and varied estate, these conditions create an operational security problem as much as a detection problem. The new capabilities below strengthen that operational foundation. They help teams verify that protection is working, introduce changes safely, and manage devices through the full lifecycle. Monitor the health of every endpoint The new health dashboard in the Defender portal shows the health of your entire endpoint estate at a glance, across Defender components and platforms. It brings health signals into one place so security teams can quickly check that Defender is deployed, connected, up to date, and operating as expected across their endpoints. If they discover devices that need attention, they can move more quickly from visibility to troubleshooting. Figure 5. Customers have asked for greater control over how Defender changes are introduced across their environments. That’s why we’re introducing new safe deployment settings that provide visibility and control over the rollout of security updates and product capabilities across Windows and Linux devices. This new experience allows security teams to validate, manage, and adopt security changes: Roll out updates progressively: New safe deployment channels allow organizations to progressively roll out Defender platform and engine updates. Teams can now validate changes on a smaller set of devices before expanding to production environments. This helps protect mission-critical systems from unexpected disruption. Adopt new security capabilities when the organization is ready: Administrators can selectively enable individual public preview features based on readiness, risk tolerance, and business requirements. Last year at Ignite, we introduced the Defender deployment tool, a lightweight tool that dynamically adapts to the operating system, delivering healthy endpoint security to a diverse estate. But just as critical as onboarding is offboarding, because attackers often try to use offboarding scripts to switch off defenses, e.g. in Octo Tempest-style intrusions. Devices need to be retired deliberately, in a controlled and traceable way. title: Vulnerability shielding: Protect the time before the patch
summary: AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery for defenders and attackers alike. An attacker can now turn a vulnerability into a working exploit within hours, but patching can’t keep pace. Our data shows that 38% of critical Patch Tuesday exposures remain unpatched for more than five days, and attackers operate in the gap between exposure and remediation. To keep up, organizations need protection that moves as fast as critical vulnerabilities are discovered, without forcing rushed patches or disrupting the business. That’s why today we’re excited to introduce vulnerability shielding in Microsoft Defender, in preview: Vulnerability shielding applies targeted, temporary protection to vulnerable systems in the gap between exposure and remediation, buying defenders time before they can apply a permanent patch. This AI-based capability reasons over the latest threat intelligence and each organization’s unique environment to choose the narrowest effective protection. Vulnerability shielding operates at two critical moments: Proactively limit exposure : The Risk Reduction Agent in Microsoft Perception as part of the Reduce exposure risk playbook creates a tailored plan for shielding vulnerabilities when patching is not immediately available or possible. Shields are time bound, reversible, choose the path of minimal business disruption, and retire automatically once the patch lands. Nothing is implemented without your approval. Protect during an active attack: When attack disruption in Microsoft Defender identifies an ongoing attack, it autonomously applies vulnerability shielding controls to exposed assets, cutting off new attack paths for adversaries and limiting the impact to your organization. Vulnerability shielding does not replace patching. Patching is the fix; shielding is designed to protect the interim risk. Autonomous protection enabled by a modern cyber stack Microsoft's cyber stack connects context, agentic reasoning, and native enforcement in a continuous loop. That integration enables vulnerability shielding to move from exposure insight to targeted protection at the speed an attack demands. Signals and context: Vulnerability shielding builds a deep, continuously updated exposure map of your environment across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, attack paths, and business context. This understanding helps determine where and how to disrupt potential attacks with the most effective protection, while preserving legitimate activity to minimize operational disruption. Actuators: Vulnerability shielding applies hardening policies tailored to each vulnerability and device, placed at the point where an attack can be cut off most effectively. It uses native enforcement controls in Microsoft Defender including reducing network reachability, restricting access paths, and tightening permissions . Agents: For preventive scenarios, green agents in Microsoft Perception can invoke vulnerability shielding when patching is not possible. They assess exposure and business impact, then recommend a coordinated plan that may combines patching, hardening, and temporary shielding. Reduce exposure. Reduce your exposure: The Risk Reduction Agent in Microsoft Perception recommends tailored vulnerability management plans. Figure 1: Reduce exposure risk playbook calling on the Risk Reduction Agent within Microsoft Perception, recommending a tailored shielding plan. Microsoft Perception helps teams act before vulnerabilities become paths to compromise. The Reduce exposure risk playbook uses the Risk Reduction Agent to prioritize risk based on exploitability, asset criticality, attack paths, patch readiness, and business impact. It then explains what matters and recommends the safest next step for security and IT teams to review. Vulnerability shielding is one of the capabilities the Risk Reduction Agent can invoke through the playbook. When a patch is available, the agent can coordinate patching through Microsoft Intune, with IT retaining control of deployment. When patching is not immediately possible e.g. because it could disrupt the business, the agent can recommend shielding. Shields apply targeted protection, buying teams time to work toward the permanent fix. The agent’s workflow is as follows: This transforms vulnerability management from a disconnected list of findings into a coordinated path from prioritization to protection. As part of public preview, the agent will provide vulnerability shielding for server-side RCE vulnerabilities, which make up 37% of vulnerabilities adversaries’ exploit. Once applied, the shield stays in place until the patch is fully deployed, then retires automatically. If you need to change course, you can roll it back with one click. Exclusions are managed through Microsoft Intune to keep critical devices and apps out of scope. You get room to remediate while staying in control of the business impact. Learn more about what else is new in Microsoft Perception . Disrupt attacks: Vulnerability shielding limits your blast radius Figure 2. Vulnerability shielding applied to a SQL server with a known public vulnerability in attack disruption Attack disruption in Microsoft Defender uses AI-powered analysis to detect and contain attacks at machine speed with over 99% confidence. It stops ransomware attacks in an average of 30 seconds. Every month Microsoft Defender disrupts about 68,000 attacks, protecting 580,000 devices from being encrypted. Utilizing the same confidence and technology, we are extending attack disruption to proactively shield vulnerabilities during ongoing attacks. On by default, attack disruption now automatically contains the exploited path and shields new routes the attacker could use - boxing them in with precise protections that reduce network reachability, restrict access paths, and tighten permissions . It acts autonomously, combining the use of the latest Threat Intelligence about vulnerabilities that are being actively exploited, as well as the unique context of an organization’s environment, to always seek the narrowest effective action and limit impact on an organization’s productivity. Crucially, the controls vulnerability shielding applies also analyze business context. Vulnerability shielding uses business context and baseline activity to understand who and what typically connects, it then applies precise network controls that block the exploit route while preserving established business traffic where possible. Security teams gain immediate protection, IT teams gain time to deploy the permanent fix safely, and finance users can keep working. Managing vulnerability shielding Shields are designed to be managed, not forgotten. Each one is temporary by design and retires once the patch is deployed, and every active shield is listed with the vulnerability it covers, the devices it applies to and why it was applied. You set the guardrails: exclude devices or apps that must never be touched, roll back any shield in one click, or turn shielding off. Before an attack, the Risk Reduction Agent simulates each shield plan against 90 days of real activity, so you see the expected impact before you approve. You can also extend shielding beyond published CVEs to vulnerabilities unique to your environment, such as in-house apps, legacy builds or AI-written code, and use your own detections to trigger the right shielding plan or attack disruption action. AI has made time the new attack surface but with vulnerability shielding organizations no longer have to choose between waiting for the patch and breaking the business. Microsoft Defender closes the exploit window in minutes, keeps you protected while you remediate, and gets out of the way when the patch lands. Vulnerability shielding is giving you protected time to patch. Disrupt attacks: Vulnerability shielding limits your blast radius Figure 2. Vulnerability shielding applied to a SQL server with a known public vulnerability in attack disruption

Every month Microsoft Defender disrupts about 68,000 attacks, protecting 580,000 devices from being encrypted. Utilizing the same confidence and technology, we are extending attack disruption to proactively shield vulnerabilities during ongoing attacks.

On by default, attack disruption now automatically contains the exploited path and shields new routes the attacker could use - boxing them in with precise protections that reduce network reachability, restrict access paths, and tighten permissions. It acts autonomously, combining the use of the latest Threat Intelligence about vulnerabilities that are being actively exploited, as well as the unique context of an organization’s environment, to always seek the narrowest effective action and limit impact on an organization’s productivity.

Crucially, the controls vulnerability shielding applies also analyze business context. Vulnerability shielding uses business context and baseline activity to understand who and what typically connects, it then applies precise network controls that block the exploit route while preserving established business traffic where possible. Security teams gain immediate protection, IT teams gain time to deploy the permanent fix safely, and finance users can keep working.

Shields are designed to be managed, not forgotten. Each one is temporary by design and retires once the patch is deployed, and every active shield is listed with the vulnerability it covers, the devices it applies to and why it was applied. You set the guardrails: exclude devices or apps that must never be touched, roll back any shield in one click, or turn shielding off. Before an attack, the Risk Reduction Agent simulates each shield plan against 90 days of real activity, so you see the expected impact before you approve. You can also extend shielding beyond published CVEs to vulnerabilities unique to your environment, such as in-house apps, legacy builds or AI-written code, and use your own detections to trigger the right shielding plan or attack disruption action.

AI has made time the new attack surface but with vulnerability shielding organizations no longer have to choose between waiting for the patch and breaking the business. Microsoft Defender closes the exploit window in minutes, keeps you protected while you remediate, and gets out of the way when the patch lands. Vulnerability shielding is giving you protected time to patch.

title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
summary: In this article Phishing attack overview Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures. Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext. If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR capabilities to investigate messages, URLs, clicks, and potential follow-on activity. Phishing attack overview Microsoft analyzed the email lures sent on November 13, 2026: the emails used the subject pattern “Outage – ” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.” Example subject line: Outage – aF7vG6 Example display names: MSF Outage Notification AMZ Service Health One example email body referenced a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12 and claimed that four messages were held after the outage. The urgency of a 24-hour deletion deadline and the prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” call to action were intended to drive immediate interaction. The activity used distinct sender domains, including: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. The messages also used email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure to generate recipient-specific URLs. In multiple samples, click-tracking links led to reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html. The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family. Figure 1. Sample of one of the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing lures. Attack chain overview Figure 2. Observed attack chain for the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing campaign. Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion. Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot. Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email. User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click. Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples. Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence. Mitigation and protection guidance Immediate actions Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack. However, organizations can consider taking the following steps: Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures. Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered. Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams. Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact. Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links. Ongoing hardening Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible. Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available. Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages. Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly. Microsoft Security Copilot Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat: Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices. Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants. Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel. Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 Outage lures to target multiple industry sectors. Advanced hunting queries These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate. Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern. let campaignDomains = dynamic([ "moments-notice.com", "em4493.moments-notice.com", "newbooker.com", "em.newbooker.com" ]); EmailEvents | where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains) or Subject matches regex @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$" | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation | order by Timestamp desc Find messages containing campaign URLs This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata. let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); EmailUrlInfo | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation | join kind=inner ( EmailEvents | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation ) on NetworkMessageId | project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId | order by Timestamp desc Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed. let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); UrlClickEvents | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain | order by Timestamp desc For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate: Unusual sign-ins New devices or user agents MFA-method changes OAuth grants Inbox or forwarding rules Delegate permissions Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data These behaviors were not observed in the source messages, they are post-click investigation targets for suspected Microsoft 365 credential phishing. MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed The activity exhibited the following techniques. Microsoft did not map credential capture, malware execution, command and control, or data exfiltration because the available evidence did not directly demonstrate those actions. Initial Access T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link | Messages contained a “RESTORE MESSAGES” link that used tracked redirect URLs and led to a non-Microsoft destination. Defense Evasion T1036 Masquerading | Messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service-health communications and used Microsoft product names and copyright language. Execution T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link | Recipients were urged to select a link within 24 hours to prevent the alleged deletion of held messages. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) The following defanged indicators were observed in the campaign and should be validated in the context of each environment before blocking. Shared service-provider infrastructure can generate false positives when used without the accompanying sender, content, and behavioral signals. Indicator Type Context moments-notice[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. planetmaison[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. em4493[.]moments-notice[.]com Domain Observed mail-from or bounce subdomain. newbooker[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. em[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed mail-from or bounce subdomain. url[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed click/open tracking host. url7489[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed click/open tracking host. u113727626[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. u118254266[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. u118250677[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. reallifeaccounting[.]com Domain Principal downstream destination observed in multiple messages. outagefixed[.]sbs Domain Downstream destination observed in some messages. outagerestored[.]sbs Domain Downstream destination observed in some messages. hxxps://reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0[.]html URL Observed destination path. hxxps://outagerestored[.]sbs/topics_pxyk/themelist0[.]html URL Observed destination path. 162[.]120[.]17[.]69:8080 IP and port Observed host for individualized /t/v3…/px[.]png resources. Outage – Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. Strengthen – Security Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. Restore — 4 messages Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family.

Figure 1. Sample of one of the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing lures. Attack chain overview Figure 2. Observed attack chain for the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing campaign.
  1. Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion.
  2. Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot.
  3. Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email.
  4. User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click.
  5. Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples.
  6. Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence.
Mitigation and protection guidance Immediate actions

Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack.

However, organizations can consider taking the following steps:

  • Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures.
  • Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered.
  • Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams.
  • Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact.
  • Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links.
Ongoing hardening
  • Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible.
  • Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.
  • Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available.
  • Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages.
  • Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly.
Microsoft Security Copilot

Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat:

  • Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices.
  • Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants.

Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 Outage lures to target multiple industry sectors.

Advanced hunting queries

These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate.

Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern

This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern.

let campaignDomains = dynamic([
    "moments-notice.com",
    "em4493.moments-notice.com",
    "newbooker.com",
    "em.newbooker.com"
]);
EmailEvents
| where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains)
    or Subject matches regex
        @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
    SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
    Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
| order by Timestamp desc

Find messages containing campaign URLs

This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
EmailUrlInfo
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
        SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName,
        Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation
) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
    SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain,
    UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc

Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs

This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed.

let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([
    "reallifeaccounting.com",
    "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click",
    "url.newbooker.com/ls/click",
    "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3."
]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload,
    NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain
| order by Timestamp desc

For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate:

  • Unusual sign-ins
  • New devices or user agents
  • MFA-method changes
  • OAuth grants
  • Inbox or forwarding rules
  • Delegate permissions
  • Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data
